questions.q: What is 'volatility clustering,' and why does it matter for financial modeling?
options: Returns themselves become perfectly predictable once volatility clusters
Large return moves tend to be followed by more large moves, making volatility forecastable even though returns themselves are not
Volatility only ever decreases over time once it starts clustering
It describes clustering of trading volume, unrelated to price moves
questions.explain: Volatility clustering is the stylized fact that periods of large moves tend to persist, and so do calm periods. This makes volatility itself a forecastable quantity, which is the whole motivation for the ARCH/GARCH family covered next.

questions.q: What is the main weakness of a simple 20-day rolling standard deviation as a volatility estimator?
options: It cannot be computed in pandas
It weights every observation in the window equally and can jump abruptly when an old observation drops out of the window
It is only defined for annualized data
It requires intraday data to compute
questions.explain: Rolling historical volatility gives equal weight to every return in the trailing window, including an old outlier, and produces an abrupt change in the estimate once that observation rolls out of the window — not a reflection of any real market event.

questions.q: How is realized volatility (RV) for a single day typically computed?
options: As the single close-to-close return for that day
As the square root of the sum of squared high-frequency intraday returns for that day
As the average of the past 252 days' closing prices
As the GARCH(1,1) conditional variance for that day
questions.explain: Realized volatility sums the squares of many high-frequency (e.g., 5-minute) returns within the day and takes the square root, giving a statistically more efficient estimate than a single daily close-to-close return.

questions.q: Why is daily volatility conventionally annualized by multiplying by sqrt(252) rather than simply by 252?
options: Because standard deviation scales with the square root of time under the typical i.i.d. returns assumption, while variance scales linearly with time
Because there are exactly 252 trading minutes in a year
Because sqrt(252) converts volatility into log-return units
Because GARCH models require this specific scaling factor
questions.explain: Under the assumption that returns are i.i.d. over time, variance scales linearly with the number of periods, so standard deviation (volatility) scales with the square root of the number of periods — hence sqrt(252) for daily-to-annual conversion.

questions.q: When intraday data is not available, what volatility estimator remains the practical default, and what does the next lesson build on top of it?
options: Realized volatility; it feeds directly into VAR models
Historical (rolling) volatility; ARCH and GARCH models build on daily-return-based volatility
Granger causality; it replaces volatility estimation entirely
Impulse response functions; they estimate volatility without any return data
questions.explain: Without high-frequency data, historical (rolling) volatility computed from daily returns is the standard default, and it is exactly the kind of input that the ARCH/GARCH models in the next two lessons are built to model and forecast.
